Daniel’s “ABS backed security backed security…” recursion is a clever Hofstadter-style “strange loop,” but it quietly smuggles in a category error: in actual securitization, an **asset-backed security is backed by a pool of underlying cash-flowing assets** (mortgages, auto loans, receivables), not by “another security” in the definitional sense. Recursion *can* happen in practice (e.g., resecuritizations like CDO-squared), but that’s a contingent market structure layered on top of securitization—not a property of “ABS” as a linguistic subclass of “asset.” If Daniel wants the analogy to bite harder, the more faithful target is not “ABS contains ABS,” but “**claims are built on claims**,” where each layer’s apparent solidity depends on conventions (ratings, haircuts, marks) rather than on new underlying cash flows—very much the territory Hofstadter was pointing at in [*Gödel, Escher, Bach*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del,_Escher,_Bach).

The swap example has a similar hidden assumption. A plain-vanilla interest-rate swap isn’t “two bonds collateralized by each other” so much as **a bilateral contract with netted cash flows**, whose credit risk is managed (or not) through collateral/margining, close-out netting, and central clearing. Seeing a swap as “bond-like” can be a useful mental model for valuation, but describing the *collateral* as “each other” risks obscuring the real mechanics: what matters in default is the legal netting set, the timing of margin calls, and the liquidity of posted collateral—features that sit outside the instrument’s abstract payoff diagram.

On 2008, Daniel’s intuition about “cycles” points in a productive direction, but the story needs one more step: the crisis wasn’t just “ABS-SPV-ABS…” as a loop; it was **maturity transformation and money-like collateral creation in the shadow banking system**, where securitized claims became repo/ABCP collateral and were treated as safe until they weren’t. That’s why the failure mode looked like a run. Gary Gorton’s account is particularly clarifying here: the core fragility was that privately produced “safe” collateral lost its unquestioned status, triggering forced deleveraging ([*Slapped by the Invisible Hand*](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/slapped-by-the-invisible-hand-9780199734156)). Framed this way, “greed and irresponsibility” may be true but incomplete: the deeper blind spot is that **the system optimized for local incentives while assuming global stability**, a very Minskyan dynamic of stability breeding instability ([Hyman Minsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyman_Minsky)).
